ManipArena: Comprehensive Real-world Evaluation of Reasoning-Oriented Generalist Robot Manipulation

Yu Sun    Meng Cao    Ping Yang    Rongtao Xu    Yunxiao Yan    Runze Xu    Liang Ma    Roy Gan    Andy Zhai    Qingxuan Chen    Zunnan Xu    Hao Wang    Jincheng Yu    Lucy Liang    Qian Wang    Ivan Laptev    Ian D Reid    Xiaodan Liang Affiliation: [
March 18, 2026
Abstract

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and world models have recently emerged as promising paradigms for general-purpose robotic intelligence, yet their progress is hindered by the lack of reliable evaluation protocols that reflect real-world deployment. Existing benchmarks are largely simulator-centric, which provide controllability but fail to capture the reality gap caused by perception noise, complex contact dynamics, hardware constraints, and system latency. Moreover, fragmented real-world evaluations across different robot platforms prevent fair and reproducible comparison. To address these challenges, we introduce ManipArena, a standardized evaluation framework designed to bridge simulation and real-world execution. ManipArena comprises 20 diverse tasks across 10,812 expert trajectories emphasizing reasoning-oriented manipulation tasks requiring semantic and spatial reasoning, supports multi-level generalization through controlled out-of-distribution settings, and incorporates long-horizon mobile manipulation beyond tabletop scenarios. The framework further provides rich sensory diagnostics, including low-level motor signals, and synchronized real-to-sim environments constructed via high-quality 3D scanning. Together, these features enable fair, realistic, and reproducible evaluation for both VLA and world model approaches, providing a scalable foundation for diagnosing and advancing embodied intelligence systems.

1 Introduction

The pursuit of scaling learning and robotics to achieve true generalization has placed Vision-Language-Action (VLA) (2, 5, 7) and world models (11) at the forefront of modern artificial intelligence. As pivotal paradigms for general-purpose robotic intelligence, these models have demonstrated promising results across diverse domains, including manipulation, mobile manipulation, and long-horizon tasks. However, the continued progress of these models critically depends on the availability of reliable and realistic evaluation protocols. Currently, the community faces a significant bottleneck: the lack of a widely adopted, fair, and realistic evaluation framework that can accurately reflect a model’s performance during real-world deployment.

The core limitation of existing evaluation paradigms lies in the profound conflict between simulator-centric assessment and real-world capability. Current evaluations are highly concentrated within simulators such as RLBench (6), VLABench (12) and Libero (8). While these environments offer essential controllability and reproducibility, they fail to account for the “reality gap” characterized by perception noise, complex contact dynamics, system latency, and hardware constraints. Consequently, success within a simulation environment cannot reliably predict performance in the physical world. Furthermore, current real-world evaluations remain fragmented; researchers often utilize disparate robot platforms and environments, making horizontal comparisons inherently unfair and results difficult to replicate. This diagnostic gap underscores the urgent need for a standardized evaluation protocol that bridges the divide between virtual training and physical execution.

To address these challenges, we introduce ManipArena, an evaluation framework built upon five core design principles to enable standardized, reasoning-heavy, and reproducible assessment for both VLA and world model approaches.

  1. 1.

    Reasoning-Oriented: ManipArena prioritizes reasoning-oriented manipulation by incorporating complex spatial constraints, multi-stage bimanual operations, and semantic understanding that go beyond simple motor skills, requiring models to demonstrate genuine execution reasoning or semantic reasoning rather than trajectory memorization.

  2. 2.

    Multi-Level Generalization: It facilitates controlled multi-level generalization through a green-screen enclosed environment with fixed lighting, systematic diversity guides for data collection, and layered out-of-distribution testing across object materials, appearances, and spatial configurations.

  3. 3.

    Mobile Manipulation: Beyond tabletop tasks, ManipArena incorporates long-horizon mobile manipulation requiring navigation, spatial memory, and sustained whole-body control across an extended workspace, providing comprehensive coverage of real-world operational scenarios.

  4. 4.

    Rich Sensory Diagnostics: The framework provides rich and open sensory signals, including low-level motor currents and joint velocities beyond standard joint states, allowing developers to perform granular force-aware action modeling and diagnostic analysis.

  5. 5.

    Real-to-Sim Synchronization: By utilizing high-quality 3D scanning, we provide synchronized real and simulated environments (Real2Sim), constructing physically consistent simulation counterparts to enable scalable evaluation and sim-to-real diagnostics without sacrificing physical realism.

2 Benchmark Design

2.1 Competition Format and Evaluation Protocol

ManipArena adopts a server-side inference architecture that fundamentally differs from existing real-robot benchmarks. Rather than requiring participants to deploy models on specific hardware, participants expose a single HTTP endpoint that accepts observation data (camera images and proprioception) and returns action commands. The organizers’ infrastructure handles all robot control, data collection, and scoring.

Crucially, ManipArena enforces a one-model-for-all-tasks rule: each participant submits a single model endpoint that is evaluated across all tasks. This is a deliberate design choice that tests genuine reasoning and generalization ability rather than task-specific overfitting—a participant cannot train 15 separate specialists, but must build one unified policy that handles pouring water, sorting headphones, inserting wires, and pressing buttons alike. This mirrors the real-world desideratum of a general-purpose manipulation system and creates a fundamentally different optimization pressure from benchmarks that allow per-task models. From the participant’s perspective, this also simplifies participation: one only needs to train and serve a single model, while the organizers handle evaluation across all tasks on all robots.

This architecture offers several additional advantages:

  • •

    Low barrier to entry: No specialized hardware required from participants.

  • •

    Reproducibility: All trials run on identical hardware under identical conditions.

  • •

    Fair comparison: No advantage from hardware optimization or latency.

  • •

    IP protection: Model weights and code are never shared with organizers.

Each task is evaluated over 10 trials. Each trial is scored on a 0–10 scale based on sub-task completion, giving a maximum of 100 points per task and a total of 1,500 points across all 15 evaluated tabletop tasks.

2.2 Task Design

ManipArena comprises 20 tasks organized into three categories: Execution Reasoning, Semantic Reasoning, and Mobile Manipulation. A deliberate design principle is that ManipArena contains no trivial tasks, i.e., every task requires reasoning, differing only in where the reasoning bottleneck lies. This distinguishes ManipArena from benchmarks that include simple pick-and-place tasks as baselines; here, even the most straightforward tasks demand precise visuomotor integration under object and spatial variation. The overview of the ManipArena benchmark is presented in Figure 3.

Tasks were selected to satisfy four criteria: (1) coverage of diverse manipulation primitives (grasping, insertion, pouring, arranging, sorting); (2) coverage of diverse object types (rigid, articulated, deformable, liquid); (3) a clear, unambiguous success criterion amenable to sub-task scoring; and (4) sufficient difficulty that no current model achieves ceiling performance, ensuring the benchmark remains discriminative.

Table 2 summarizes all 20 tasks and Figure 1 shows representative examples from each category. Detailed per-task attribute diversity, spatial configurations, and OOD object specifications are provided in Appendix 5.

2.2.1 Execution Reasoning Tasks (10 tasks)

The challenge of this type of tasks lies in how to execute—grasp strategy, force control, and bimanual coordination. These tasks test whether a model can translate a known goal into precise, adaptive motor behavior across varied object instances and spatial configurations.

2.2.2 Semantic Reasoning Tasks (5 tasks)

The challenge of this type of tasks lies in what to do—understanding object categories, attributes, and relations before acting. A model that pattern-matches to training object appearances will fail when presented with novel instances of the same semantic category. These tasks create a clean diagnostic: if a model fails, it is because it cannot resolve the semantic ambiguity, not because it lacks motor skill.

2.2.3 Mobile Manipulation Tasks (5 tasks)

Mobile tasks require long-horizon whole-body control across an extended workspace, demanding navigation, spatial memory, and sustained task execution over 2–3 minutes. They are on average 4.3×\times longer than tabletop tasks (2,878 vs. 665 avg frames at 20 fps) and account for 60.6% of total dataset frames despite comprising only 26.7% of trajectories. This length difference makes them particularly challenging for current VLA architectures with fixed context windows.

2.3 Controlled Evaluation Environment

A fundamental challenge in real-robot benchmarks is attribution: when a model fails on a new trial, is it because the object changed, the layout changed, or simply because the background lighting shifted? Most existing benchmarks evaluate in open environments where all these factors vary simultaneously, making it impossible to attribute performance differences to specific generalization axes. A second challenge is reproducibility: real-world lab environments change over time—furniture is moved, lighting conditions shift with weather and time of day, and clutter accumulates on work surfaces—making it difficult to reproduce evaluation conditions weeks or months later, let alone across different sites.

ManipArena addresses both challenges by conducting all evaluations inside a green-screen enclosed environment—a self-contained booth with uniform chroma-key walls and ceiling. This design provides three key properties:

Variable isolation. By fixing the background to a uniform surface, we eliminate uncontrolled visual variation. Performance differences across trials can only arise from object-level or spatial-level changes that we explicitly design, transforming the benchmark from a black-box leaderboard into a controlled experiment where generalization is measurable and attributable.

Controlled illumination. The enclosure uses fixed artificial lighting with constant color temperature and intensity, shielding the workspace from external light sources (windows, overhead lab lights, seasonal daylight variation). This eliminates a confound that plagues open-environment benchmarks: apparent performance drops caused not by policy failure but by shadow shifts, specular highlights, or white-balance changes that alter the visual appearance of objects and surfaces.

Reproducibility and portability. Because the booth is self-contained, the entire evaluation environment can be relocated or replicated without affecting visual conditions. Moving the setup to a different room, building, or institution preserves identical background and lighting—the only requirement is re-placing the task objects according to the diversity guide. This also enables longitudinal consistency: evaluations conducted weeks apart produce visually identical conditions, a property that open labs cannot guarantee. For competitions, this means a booth at one site produces results directly comparable to a booth at another site, enabling decentralized evaluation without sacrificing reproducibility.

For mobile manipulation tasks, the green-screen enclosure additionally defines the physical workspace boundary (∼\sim3 m ×\times 3 m), ensuring consistent navigation conditions across all trials.

Future extensibility. The chroma-key background is not merely a practical convenience—it opens a systematic avenue for visual robustness research. By compositing natural scene backgrounds onto the green screen in post-processing or via real-time projection, researchers can introduce controlled background variation as an independent experimental variable—testing, for instance, whether a policy trained in the green-screen booth transfers to a kitchen background, an industrial setting, or adversarial textures, all without physically moving the robot.

2.4 Systematic Diversity Design

Within the controlled visual environment established by the green screen, we systematically inject diversity into the training data so that high scores must come from genuine generalization, not memorization. Unlike benchmarks where training data diversity arises incidentally from natural collection, ManipArena treats diversity as a designed experimental variable. Each task is accompanied by a diversity guide—a structured specification that defines the exact object variants, color sets, spatial configurations, and (for semantic tasks) compositional permutations to be covered. Trained operators collect approximately 500 trajectories per task (10,812 total across 20 tasks, ∼\sim188 hours) following these guides, with each diversity dimension kept approximately uniformly distributed (within 10–15% of equal distribution) to prevent models from exploiting frequency biases.

A critical design constraint is the strict separation between training and test distributions: OOD test objects are never present in the training data. For example, put_spoon_to_bowl trains on stainless steel and children’s spoons but tests on a black plastic spoon; sort_headphone trains on wired, over-ear, and bluetooth types but tests on a neckband headphone. This separation ensures that models cannot achieve high OOD scores through memorization—they must genuinely generalize.

We organize training diversity into three hierarchical levels, each targeting a different generalization axis. Each task includes 2–7 explicitly controlled diversity dimensions across these levels.

Level 1—Physical Attribute Diversity (appearance layer). Within each task, objects vary along material, color, and size dimensions with systematic coverage. For example, arrange_cup includes both ceramic mugs and paper cups in red and white (2 materials ×\times 2 colors); pour_water uses glass, paper, and ceramic cups with left/right handle orientations; put_glasses covers adult and children’s frames; insert_wireline uses white and black wires. In total, Level 1 diversity produces dozens to hundreds of unique object configurations per task.

Level 2—Spatial Configuration Diversity (layout layer). Object positions and orientations are randomized across the workspace according to the per-task diversity guide, preventing models from learning fixed-position trajectories. Specifically, insert_wireline varies socket position (L/R/C) ×\times wire position (U/M/D) == 9 unique spatial combinations; pour_water varies handle direction (L/R) ×\times cup position (6 zones) == 12 combinations; put_ring_onto_rod varies rod and ring positions across 7+ configurations; pick_items_into_basket varies basket position (L/C/R) ×\times item sets. Tasks with more diversity dimensions—such as put_blocks_to_color (7 dimensions) and put_items_into_drawer (6 dimensions)—span particularly large configuration spaces.

Level 3—Semantic Composition Diversity (task layer). For semantic reasoning tasks, the semantic content itself varies across trials—different object combinations, orderings, and category assignments. press_button_in_order uses permutations of 4 colors (pink, yellow, blue, green), yielding 24 possible sequences; pick_fruits_into_basket draws subsets from {apple, pear, grape, banana, bread, lettuce}; pair_up_items samples from different glove and sock combinations (glove1–3, sock1–2); classify_items_as_shape varies the ordering of shape categories. This level of diversity is unique to semantic reasoning tasks and is critical for preventing models from memorizing fixed task configurations.

These three levels are hierarchically ordered: Level 1 tests perceptual generalization (can the model handle a different-looking object?), Level 2 tests spatial generalization (can it handle a new layout?), and Level 3 tests semantic generalization (can it handle a new task configuration?). Full diversity specifications per task are provided in Appendix 6. Crucially, this designed training diversity is a necessary condition for meaningful OOD evaluation—without sufficiently diverse training data, OOD trials would merely test interpolation within a narrow distribution rather than genuine extrapolation beyond it. In Figure 5, we demonstrate some typical diversity designs.

2.5 Stratified OOD Evaluation Design

The 10 evaluation trials per task are not randomly configured. They follow a stratified structure with increasing generalization difficulty: trials T1–T4 test in-domain competence with training-distribution objects in varied positions; T5–T8 introduce visual shifts—appearance changes (e.g., different shape or color) within the training distribution; and T9–T10 present semantic OOD objects unseen during training. For example, in put_spoon_to_bowl, T1–T4 use a stainless steel spoon, T5–T8 use a children’s spoon (different shape), and T9–T10 use a black plastic spoon (new material and color).

This structure enables a complete generalization profile from a single evaluation session—one can directly compare a model’s performance across three generalization levels and compute the degradation curve without running separate experiments.

Semantic distance determines OOD difficulty. Not all OOD is equally difficult. We deliberately include OOD objects at varying semantic distances from the training distribution—from near-OOD (e.g., goggles for the glasses task, preserving grasp strategy) to far-OOD (e.g., neckband headphones, requiring fundamentally different recognition). This allows us to test the hypothesis that OOD generalization difficulty is determined by semantic distance, not merely by the binary in/out-of-distribution distinction.

Compounding OOD factors. Several tasks are designed so that OOD trials change multiple factors simultaneously, testing whether generalization degrades gracefully or catastrophically. For example, in sort_headphone, T7–8 change only the headphone type (bluetooth, still black)—single-factor OOD; T9–10 change both type (neckband) and color (white)—compound OOD. Similarly, in put_spoon_to_bowl, OOD trials change both material (plastic) and color (black) simultaneously. This design enables disentangling the individual and combined effects of OOD factors on model performance (see Section 4 for quantitative analysis).

Configuration-level generalization. For the remaining 8 tasks where T9–T10 do not introduce new object types, the 10 trials systematically cover the spatial and compositional configuration space within the training distribution. For example, pick_items_into_basket varies basket position (right →\to center →\to left) across trials, and press_button_in_order permutes color sequences. These trials test whether models are robust to layout and semantic composition changes—a prerequisite for reliable real-world deployment even without OOD objects.

Detailed per-trial specifications are provided in Appendix 7.

Controlled generalization through three pillars. The green-screen environment, systematic diversity design, and stratified OOD evaluation form an integrated framework for controlled generalization measurement. The green screen eliminates uncontrolled visual confounders, ensuring that performance differences are attributable to the variables we design. The diversity guides ensure that training data covers a sufficiently broad distribution, so that OOD evaluation tests genuine extrapolation rather than interpolation. The stratified trial structure then measures generalization at multiple difficulty levels within a single evaluation session. Together, these three pillars make ManipArena not merely a task collection with a leaderboard, but a controlled experimental platform for diagnosing where and why generalization succeeds or fails.

2.6 Robot Platform

All tasks use the X2Robot bimanual system—a unified embodiment across all 20 tasks. By eliminating embodiment variation, performance differences reflect policy capability rather than hardware differences. Figure 6 shows both the tabletop and mobile configurations within the green-screen enclosure.

Tabletop setup: 4 robot units, each equipped with bimanual 6-DOF follower arms, a master-follower teleoperation interface, and 3 camera views (face, left wrist, right wrist). Fixed studio lighting (LED panel and softbox) ensures consistent illumination across all trials. Each unit collects approximately one quarter of the training data per task. Evaluation of tabletop manipulation is also distributed across these same 4 units, ensuring that models are tested on the exact platforms from which the training data originates (c.f. Figure 7).

Mobile setup: 1 Quanta X1 mobile robot with bimanual ARX arms mounted on a mecanum-wheel omnidirectional base. A height-adjustable lifting column allows the robot to adapt its working height for different tasks (e.g., reaching a high shelf vs. picking items from the floor). A head-mounted camera provides the global view, complemented by wrist cameras on each arm. The robot navigates and manipulates within the ∼\sim3 m ×\times 3 m green-screen enclosure.

The single-embodiment design makes ManipArena a clean testbed for multi-task training strategies: all 15 tabletop tasks share identical action spaces, joint limits, and kinematics, so any performance difference between task-specific and unified models reflects learning dynamics, not embodiment mismatch.

2.7 Sensor Data and Action Space

ManipArena provides 56-dimensional state and action per frame for tabletop tasks (62D for mobile tasks), richer than standard LeRobot format. Each 56D vector comprises: end-effector poses (position, rotation, gripper =7​D×2=7\text{D}\times 2 arms =14​D=14\text{D}), joint positions (7​D×2=14​D7\text{D}\times 2=14\text{D}), joint velocities (7​D×2=14​D7\text{D}\times 2=14\text{D}), and joint currents (7​D×2=14​D7\text{D}\times 2=14\text{D}, where the last dimension of each arm is the gripper current). Mobile tasks add 6 extra dimensions: head rotation (2D), lifting column height (1D), and base velocity in xx, yy, θ\theta (3D). The full data collection records 112D per frame (follow + master arms); the open-source release provides the follow-arm subset for direct policy training (see Appendix 8).

The inclusion of motor current and joint velocity data is a deliberate design choice. Motor currents serve as a torque proxy—critical for contact-rich tasks such as pour_water (sensing liquid weight), insert_wireline (detecting insertion contact), and arrange_cup (avoiding excessive force). Joint velocities capture dynamic motion profiles that complement static position information. Current VLA and world model baselines do not utilize these signals, and we provide them to encourage research on force-aware and dynamics-aware policies.

Three camera views (face, left wrist, right wrist) provide complementary perspectives: the face camera captures the global workspace, while wrist cameras provide close-up views critical for precision tasks.

2.8 Real2Sim

To enable scalable offline evaluation and sim-to-real transfer research, we construct digitally twinned simulation environments that are geometrically and visually consistent with the physical evaluation setup (Figure 8).

Simulation platform. The simulation environment is built on IsaacLab and IsaacLab-Arena, providing high-fidelity physics simulation with GPU-accelerated parallel environments. This enables large-scale policy evaluation and reinforcement learning experiments that would be prohibitively expensive on physical hardware.

Scene reconstruction. The physical workspace—including the green-screen enclosure, tables, shelves, and fixtures—is reconstructed using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), capturing both geometry and appearance with photorealistic fidelity. This ensures that the visual observations in simulation closely match those from the real cameras.

Object generation. Task objects (cups, spoons, headphones, etc.) are generated using Hunyuan3D, producing high-quality 3D assets with accurate geometry and texture. These assets are imported into the simulation environment with appropriate physical properties (mass, friction, collision meshes).

Trajectory alignment. The simulation data is directly aligned with real-robot trajectories: we replay the recorded real-robot joint trajectories in simulation, producing paired real-sim observation sequences. This tight alignment enables precise sim-to-real gap analysis—researchers can compare model behavior on identical trajectories in both domains to isolate the sources of transfer failure.

2.9 Evaluation Scoring

Each task is decomposed into ordered sub-tasks, and evaluation uses partial credit scoring: a trial that completes 7 out of 10 sub-tasks receives a score of 7, not 0. This provides richer signal than binary success/failure—it reveals where in the task pipeline a model fails, not just whether it fails.

Scoring examples. Consider pour_water_from_bottle (5 sub-tasks): (1) grasp the bottle, (2) lift the bottle, (3) move to pouring position above the cup, (4) tilt and pour water, (5) return the bottle upright. A model that grasps and lifts the bottle but fails to pour receives 3/10 rather than 0—clearly distinguishing it from a model that cannot even grasp. Similarly, put_items_into_drawer has 10 sub-tasks spanning opening the drawer, picking each item, placing it inside, and closing the drawer; partial credit reveals whether failures occur at the drawer-manipulation stage or the object-grasping stage.

Sub-task complexity varies dramatically across tasks: press_button_in_order has 5 sub-tasks (avg 18.4 s per trial), while put_clothes_in_hamper has 14 sub-tasks (avg 193.6 s). Each trial is scored out of 10, each task out of 100 (10 trials), and the overall competition score sums to 1,500 across 15 evaluated tabletop tasks.

The combination of sub-task scoring and stratified trial structure produces a rich diagnostic matrix: for each task, we obtain a 10-trial ×\times NN-sub-task score grid, segmented into three generalization levels (in-domain, visual shift, semantic OOD). This enables fine-grained analysis—for instance, one can determine that a model consistently fails at sub-task 4 (pouring) across all OOD trials but succeeds at grasping, pinpointing the generalization bottleneck to force control rather than object recognition.

3 Dataset

3.1 Overview

The ManipArena training dataset comprises 10,812 teleoperated trajectories collected across 20 tasks (∼\sim188 hours at 20 fps). All data was collected via a master-follower bimanual setup: human operators demonstrated tasks on the master arms while the follower arms executed the motions on the robot. Four tabletop robots collected data in parallel, each contributing approximately one quarter of the trajectories per task (∼\sim125 trajectories per robot per task). The mobile robot collected all 5 mobile task trajectories independently.

Each trajectory consists of:

  • •

    Three synchronized video streams (face, left wrist, right wrist) at 640×\times480 resolution, 20 fps.

  • •

    Proprioceptive state (56D for tabletop, 62D for mobile) at 20 Hz: joint positions, joint velocities, motor currents, end-effector poses, and gripper states.

  • •

    Action labels: same modalities as state, recorded from the follow arms.

  • •

    Language instruction: a natural-language description of the task goal (e.g., “Arrange the cups into an inverted triangle”).

Data collection followed the per-task diversity guides described in Section 2.4: operators were instructed to cover all specified object variants, spatial configurations, and (for semantic tasks) compositional permutations. The resulting distribution across diversity dimensions is approximately uniform, verified during collection via automated monitoring.

3.2 Per-Task Statistics

Table 3 summarizes the dataset statistics per task category. Per-task breakdowns are provided in Appendix 5.

The three categories exhibit markedly different episode length profiles. Semantic reasoning tasks have the shortest episodes (avg 25.0 s) despite requiring higher cognitive complexity—the manipulation itself is simple once the semantic ambiguity is resolved. Execution reasoning tasks are longer (avg 39.2 s), reflecting more complex motor sequences. Mobile manipulation tasks are 4.3×\times longer than tabletop tasks on average (143.9 s), dominated by navigation overhead and multi-step object transport. Despite comprising only 26.7% of trajectories, mobile tasks account for 60.6% of total frames.

This episode length disparity has practical implications for model training. Mobile tasks generate disproportionately large data volumes per trajectory, and their long-horizon structure challenges VLA architectures with fixed context windows.

3.3 Data Format and Open Release

All data is released in LeRobot v2.1 format, a standardized structure for robot learning datasets. Each task is packaged as an independent dataset with the following structure:

  • •

    meta/info.json — dataset metadata (episode count, feature dimensions, fps, splits).

  • •

    meta/episodes.jsonl — per-episode metadata (language instruction, episode length).

  • •

    meta/tasks.jsonl — task descriptions in natural language.

  • •

    data/chunk-{id}/episode_{id}.parquet — proprioceptive state and action data (56D per frame).

  • •

    videos/chunk-{id}/{camera}/episode_{id}.mp4 — compressed video streams for each of the three camera views.

The open release includes all 20 tasks (15 tabletop + 5 mobile; 10,812 episodes total) in LeRobot v2.1 format. Tabletop tasks use 56D state/action vectors; mobile tasks use 62D (56D + 6D for head rotation, lifting height, and base velocity).

The action and state vectors are each 56-dimensional, organized as follows for the bimanual follow arms:

  • •

    End-effector poses (14D): Cartesian position (3D), rotation (3D), and gripper state (1D) for each arm.

  • •

    Joint positions (14D): 7-DOF per arm (6 arm joints + 1 gripper joint).

  • •

    Joint velocities (14D): Joint angular velocity per joint—captures dynamic motion profiles.

  • •

    Joint currents (14D): Motor torque proxy per joint (last dimension per arm is gripper current)—critical for force-sensitive tasks.

For mobile manipulation tasks, 6 additional dimensions are provided: head rotation (2D), lifting column height (1D), and base velocity (xx, yy, θ\theta; 3D), yielding 62D per frame. This modular layout allows participants to select task-relevant subsets (e.g., end-effector-only control with 14D, or full joint-level control with 56D/62D). The LeRobot format ensures direct compatibility with popular VLA training frameworks, allowing participants to load data with minimal preprocessing.

4 Baseline Experiments

To diagnose the capability boundaries of current embodied AI approaches, we evaluate three representative baselines on all 15 tabletop tasks, spanning two dominant paradigms: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAM). Evaluation of the 5 mobile manipulation tasks is ongoing and will be reported in a subsequent update.

4.1 Baseline Models

π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Single (task-specific VLA). π0.5\pi_{0.5} (5) is a state-of-the-art VLA model combining a pre-trained vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action head. It is pre-trained on heterogeneous multi-robot data with semantic subtask prediction, then post-trained via flow matching for continuous action generation. In the Single configuration, we fine-tune an independent π0.5\pi_{0.5} on each task, yielding 15 task-specific specialists.

π0.5\pi_{0.5}-OneModel (unified multi-task VLA). A single π0.5\pi_{0.5} trained jointly on all 15 tabletop tasks. This tests ManipArena’s one-model-for-all-tasks paradigm: the model must share representations across tasks from millimeter-precision insertion to semantic object sorting. Comparing OneModel with Single isolates the effect of multi-task training on a fixed architecture.

DreamZero (World Action Model). DreamZero (11) takes a fundamentally different approach: it learns a joint video-action generative model via autoregressive video diffusion. Rather than directly predicting actions, it “dreams” future video frames and extracts actions from the generated sequence, learning physical dynamics as an intermediate representation.

All baselines receive identical inputs (three camera views and proprioceptive state) and output 14D end-effector pose actions (Cartesian position, rotation, and gripper state for each arm) via the server-side inference protocol. Although ManipArena provides the full 56D state (including joint velocities and motor currents), all three baselines in this evaluation use only the end-effector representation for action prediction. A trial is considered successful if the score ≥\geq9 out of 10.

Inference latency. The two paradigms exhibit drastically different computational costs. On a single NVIDIA A800 GPU, π0.5\pi_{0.5} (both Single and OneModel) achieves ∼\sim110 ms per action step, enabling near-real-time control at ∼\sim9 Hz. DreamZero, due to its autoregressive video generation pipeline, requires ∼\sim7–8 s per step on a single A800 and ∼\sim4–5 s on two A800s—roughly 50–70×\times slower than VLA inference. This latency difference reflects the inherently higher computational cost of autoregressive video generation compared to direct action prediction.

4.2 Overall Results

Table 4 presents the complete results across all 15 tabletop tasks. Several high-level observations emerge from the data:

The benchmark remains far from saturated. The best overall score is 640.5 out of 1,500 (42.7%), achieved by OneModel. Even the single best task performance—DreamZero’s 97.8 on pick_items_into_basket—is an outlier; the median per-task best score across all models is 51.5. Four tasks remain below 30 for all models (pour_water: 19, insert_wireline: 24, arrange_cup: 25, put_stationery: 26), indicating that these tasks pose fundamental challenges beyond the capabilities of current approaches.

No single model dominates. OneModel wins on 7 of 15 tasks, π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Single wins on 3, and DreamZero wins on 4 (with 1 tie). The three models exhibit low pairwise correlation (π0.5\pi_{0.5} vs. DreamZero: r=0.34r{=}0.34; π0.5\pi_{0.5} vs. OneModel: r=0.74r{=}0.74; OneModel vs. DreamZero: r=0.43r{=}0.43), indicating that performance on one task is a poor predictor of performance on another—different models excel on different task types, underscoring the value of evaluating across a diverse task suite.

4.3 Single-Task vs. Multi-Task VLA

Comparing π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Single (626.3) with OneModel (640.5) on the same architecture reveals a nuanced trade-off between cross-task transfer and task-specific knowledge retention.

4.3.1 Multi-Task Gains: Semantic Recognition Transfer

OneModel substantially outperforms Single on tasks requiring object-level semantic understanding: sort_headphone (73 vs. 35, ++109%), pair_up_items (51.5 vs. 21, ++145%), and pick_fruits (94 vs. 90). As shown in Figure 10(b), this advantage concentrates on semantic reasoning tasks (OneModel avg 58.9 vs. Single avg 50.6), while execution tasks show comparable performance (34.6 vs. 37.3). The common thread is that these tasks require distinguishing object categories—headphone types, matching pairs, fruits versus non-fruits—and multi-task training exposes the model to a broader variety of objects across tasks, building richer shared visual representations that transfer to categorical recognition.

4.3.2 Multi-Task Costs: Procedural Knowledge Forgetting

Conversely, OneModel suffers severe degradation on tasks that require task-specific procedural reasoning: press_button_in_order (13 vs. 48, −-73%) and put_items_into_drawer (7 vs. 34, −-79%). These tasks share a distinctive structure: the model must read a visual instruction on the table (a color-sequence card for press_button; the three-drawer category mapping for put_items_drawer) and execute a specific procedure conditioned on that instruction. Single-task fine-tuning can memorize these task-specific input-output mappings, but multi-task training dilutes them across 15 tasks. Notably, on press_button, OneModel scores exactly 1 point on 8 out of 10 trials—suggesting that it has lost the procedural policy entirely and defaults to a minimal behavior, while Single at least attempts the correct sequence and occasionally succeeds (T1=10, T10=10).

4.3.3 Summary

Multi-task training produces a clear trade-off: it enhances cross-task visual recognition (beneficial for semantic reasoning) at the cost of task-specific procedural memory (detrimental for instruction-conditioned sequential tasks). This finding has practical implications for competition participants: a unified model benefits from diverse visual co-training but may require task-specific adaptation mechanisms to retain procedural knowledge.

4.4 VLA vs. World Action Model

We compare OneModel (the unified VLA representing ManipArena’s competition format) against DreamZero (the world action model) to diagnose the capability boundaries of the two paradigms. Their cross-task correlation is low (r=0.43r=0.43), confirming fundamentally different learned strategies. We analyze their complementary profiles along four dimensions.

4.4.1 Coarse-Grained Success, Fine-Grained Failure

DreamZero’s performance reveals a consistent pattern: it can execute coarse pick-and-place operations but fails at fine-grained manipulation in later sub-task stages.

On pick_items_into_basket, which requires only picking objects and dropping them into a basket, DreamZero achieves 97.8/100 with 90% SR—far exceeding OneModel’s 37/100. Yet on tasks requiring precision in the final sub-steps, the roles reverse:

  • •

    insert_wireline: DreamZero scores exactly 3 on 8 out of 10 trials. Given the scoring rubric (left-hand pick cable: 3pts →\to right-hand receive: 3pts →\to insert: 3pts →\to retract: 1pt), the fixed score of 3 indicates completion of only the first sub-step. OneModel scores similarly overall (21/100) but with more varied per-trial patterns.

  • •

    sort_headphone: DreamZero achieves 9/10 on 6 trials, consistently missing only arm retraction (1pt)—likely because retraction produces minimal visual change in the video prediction objective. OneModel achieves full 10/10 on 7 trials, demonstrating that VLA’s direct action supervision captures even low-visual-signal behaviors.

  • •

    put_glasses: DreamZero scores 0% SR (37/100) while OneModel achieves 70% SR (87/100). The bottleneck is the final bimanual shelf-placement step—coarse planning suffices for pickup but not for coordinated dual-arm precision.

This contrast is striking: on the same robot with the same tasks, OneModel excels where precision matters (put_glasses: 87) while DreamZero dominates where coarse planning suffices (pick_items: 97.8). World models learn effective coarse-grained planning through video prediction—gross object movements produce large visual signals—but lack the fine-grained motor control that VLA models achieve through direct action supervision.

4.4.2 Semantic Understanding Gap

OneModel achieves a semantic-task average of 58.9 versus DreamZero’s 32.7, but this aggregate gap masks a more nuanced pattern across individual tasks.

On tasks where the language instruction fully specifies the task objective—sort_headphone (“put headphones into the basket”) and pick_fruits (“pick fruits into the basket”)—DreamZero scores 66 and 45 respectively, remaining competitive with VLA models. The semantic challenge in these tasks reduces to object-level recognition, and the manipulation itself is straightforward pick-and-place.

However, on tasks where the language instruction only provides a high-level goal and the model must extract the concrete action plan from visual cues in the scene—press_button_in_order (read a printed color-sequence card to determine which buttons to press) and pair_up_items (infer matching rules from the displayed object arrangement)—DreamZero scores only 3 and 13.5, while OneModel achieves 13 and 51.5.

This pattern suggests that the performance gap depends on whether the task objective is fully specified by the language instruction or must be additionally inferred from visual context. When language alone suffices to define the goal, world models remain competitive; when the model must ground scene-level visual information into a concrete action sequence, VLA models show a clearer advantage—though neither paradigm demonstrates robust performance across all semantic task types.

4.4.3 Generalization: OOD Robustness and Spatial Invariance

Despite its lower overall score, DreamZero exhibits markedly different generalization behavior from VLA models.

Compound OOD. On sort_headphone’s four-level progression (Figure 11), OneModel degrades from 10.0 (in-domain) to 0.5 (neckband + white, −-95%), while DreamZero degrades only from 6.7 to 4.5 (−-33%). This striking gap suggests that the world model’s video-based representations capture physical affordances (shape, graspability) that are less sensitive to surface-level appearance changes than VLA’s observation-action mappings.

Spatial invariance. On pick_items_into_basket (Figure 10a), where the basket position shifts from right to left across trials, DreamZero maintains near-perfect performance (right: 10.0, center: 10.0, left: 9.25; only −-8%). OneModel degrades sharply from 4.05 to 2.25 (−-44%). This position-invariance likely arises because DreamZero’s video prediction objective implicitly learns spatial equivariance—predicting future frames requires understanding that the same manipulation works regardless of absolute position—while OneModel’s direct action mapping is more sensitive to absolute spatial coordinates.

Brittle OOD: spatial configuration, not object identity. On put_spoon_to_bowl, T9 and T10 use the identical OOD object (black plastic spoon) in different spatial configurations. OneModel scores 0 on T9 but 4 on T10; π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Single shows the opposite pattern (T9=10, T10=0). The two VLA models have learned different spatial biases, and their OOD “generalization” is simply accidental alignment with one configuration—not true understanding of the novel object. DreamZero shows a similar pattern (T9=6, T10=0), suggesting that even world models are not immune to spatial configuration sensitivity on precision tasks.

4.4.4 Capability Boundary Analysis

To systematically characterize each model’s strengths and weaknesses, we classify the sub-task types that appear across all 15 tasks into five core capability dimensions and assess each model’s performance on each (Figure 12):

  • •

    Coarse Manipulation: grasping objects and placing them in large target areas. DreamZero dominates (pick_items: 97.8 vs. OneModel 37), benefiting from video prediction’s natural affinity for gross object movements.

  • •

    Precision Manipulation: precise placement, bimanual coordination, and force control. OneModel leads (put_glasses: 87 vs. DreamZero 37), while four tasks remain below 30 for all models (pour_water: 19, insert_wireline: 24), identifying force-sensitive fine manipulation as the key open frontier.

  • •

    Sequential Reasoning: multi-step procedures conditioned on visual instructions. π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Single excels (press_button: 48 vs. OneModel 13 vs. DreamZero 3), demonstrating that task-specific fine-tuning captures procedural knowledge that multi-task training erases.

  • •

    Semantic Understanding: object recognition, category sorting, and attribute matching. OneModel leads (4-task avg 70.4 vs. π0.5\pi_{0.5} 51.2 vs. DreamZero 40.1), benefiting from cross-task visual representation transfer.

  • •

    Spatial Robustness: consistency across spatial configurations. DreamZero is nearly position-invariant (within-task std 1.68 vs. π0.5\pi_{0.5} 2.58; basket position shift −-8% vs. VLA −-44% to −-57%).

Each model has a unique “Strong” dimension with no model dominating all five, confirming that VLA and WAM learn complementary capabilities.

4.5 Diagnostic Value of Partial Credit Scoring

ManipArena’s sub-task scoring reveals critical distinctions that binary success/failure metrics would obscure. Under a binary criterion, all three models appear similar—each achieves SR>>50% on only 1–2 tasks. However, partial credit reveals qualitatively different failure modes:

  • •

    DreamZero on insert_wireline: SR=0%, but avg 2.4/trial →\to consistently completes the first sub-step (cable pickup).

  • •

    DreamZero on sort_headphone: SR=60%, with six trials scoring 9/10 →\to completes the full manipulation but omits arm retraction.

  • •

    OneModel on press_button: SR=0%, avg 1.3/trial →\to the model has essentially lost the task-specific policy.

  • •

    π0.5\pi_{0.5} on press_button: SR=20%, avg 4.8/trial →\to actively attempts the sequence with occasional success.

These distinctions—“cannot start” versus “completes partially” versus “succeeds intermittently”—provide actionable diagnostic signals that inform model improvement strategies.

4.6 Summary

Our evaluation reveals three actionable insights for the field:

  1. 1.

    Multi-task VLA training enhances semantic recognition via cross-task transfer (++109% on sort_headphone) but erases task-specific procedural knowledge (−-73% on press_button). Future architectures should preserve procedural memory while enabling semantic sharing.

  2. 2.

    World Action Models exhibit a complementary profile to VLAs: superior spatial invariance (−-8% vs. −-57%) and graceful OOD degradation (−-33% vs. −-95%), but limited to coarse-grained manipulation (97.8 on pick-place, 0% SR on precision tasks). Combining VLA-style precise action generation with WAM-style physical reasoning is a promising direction.

  3. 3.

    Force-sensitive fine manipulation (pouring, insertion, zipping) remains an open challenge for both paradigms—the best score on these tasks is 26/100—identifying this as the frontier where novel approaches leveraging ManipArena’s motor current and joint velocity data may yield breakthroughs.

5 Task Details

This appendix provides the full specification for each of the 20 ManipArena tasks, including the sub-task decomposition, scoring rubric, object variants used in training, and per-trial evaluation configurations.

5.1 Execution Reasoning Tasks

5.1.1 arrange_cup_inverted_triangle

Goal: Arrange three cups into an inverted triangle formation (two cups on the bottom row, one on top).

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Pick up 1st cup (1) →\to Place upside-down at center (1) →\to Pick up 2nd cup (1) →\to Place next to 1st (2) →\to Pick up 3rd cup (1) →\to Stack on top of two cups (3) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Ceramic mug (red, white), paper cup (red, white).
OOD objects: Plastic cup (blue, green — unseen material + color).

Per-trial configuration:

Trial Cup Type Color Positions OOD Level
T1 Mug Red L / UR / R In-domain
T2 Mug Red UL / TC / BC In-domain
T3 Mug White TC / L / BC In-domain
T4 Mug White R / UR / R In-domain
T5 Paper cup Red L / R / UL Visual shift
T6 Paper cup Red UR / BC / BC Visual shift
T7 Paper cup White BC / UR / LL Visual shift
T8 Paper cup White TC / UR / LL Visual shift
T9 Plastic cup Blue LL / R / BC Semantic OOD
T10 Plastic cup Red UR / R / BC Semantic OOD

5.1.2 put_spoon_to_bowl

Goal: Pick up a bowl, place it at the table center, then pick up a spoon and place it inside the bowl.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Pick up bowl (2) →\to Place bowl at center (2) →\to Pick up spoon (2) →\to Place spoon in bowl (3) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Stainless steel spoon (white/silver), children’s spoon (white).
OOD objects: Black plastic spoon (new material + new color).

Per-trial configuration:

Trial Spoon Type Color Spoon Pos Handle Dir OOD Level
T1 Stainless steel White R UL In-domain
T2 Stainless steel White R UR In-domain
T3 Stainless steel White LR L In-domain
T4 Stainless steel White BC LL In-domain
T5 Children’s White R UR Visual shift
T6 Children’s White TC TC Visual shift
T7 Children’s White R UR Visual shift
T8 Children’s White UL LR Visual shift
T9 Plastic Black TC UL Semantic OOD
T10 Plastic Black LR TC Semantic OOD

5.1.3 put_glasses_on_woodshelf

Goal: Pick up glasses, adjust orientation at table center, then use both grippers to place them on a wooden shelf.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Pick up glasses (2) →\to Place at table center (2) →\to Adjust orientation (2) →\to Bimanual grasp & place on shelf (3) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Adult eyeglass frames, children’s frames, safety goggles.
OOD objects: Sunglasses (different folding mechanism + style).

Per-trial configuration:

Trial Glasses Type Position Direction OOD Level
T1 Adult frame Lower-left Right In-domain
T2 Adult frame Upper-left Left In-domain
T3 Adult frame Lower-left Up In-domain
T4 Children’s frame Upper-right Left Visual shift
T5 Children’s frame Upper-right Right Visual shift
T6 Children’s frame Lower-left Right Visual shift
T7 Safety goggles Lower-right Right Visual shift
T8 Safety goggles Lower-left Right Visual shift
T9 Sunglasses Upper-right Down Semantic OOD
T10 Sunglasses Upper-left Up Semantic OOD

5.1.4 put_ring_onto_rod

Goal: Move the rod to the table center, then pick up a ring-shaped object and thread it onto the rod.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Move rod to center (3) →\to Pick up ring (3) →\to Thread onto rod (3) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Circular ring, square ring (brown).
OOD objects: Triangular ring (white — new shape + color).

5.1.5 put_items_into_drawer

Goal: Sort three items into the correct drawers of a 3-layer cabinet: stationery in drawer 1, electronics in drawer 2, toys in drawer 3.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Open drawer 1 (1) →\to Place stationery (1) →\to Close drawer 1 (1) →\to Open drawer 2 (1) →\to Place electronics (1) →\to Close drawer 2 (1) →\to Open drawer 3 (1) →\to Place toy (1) →\to Close drawer 3 (1) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Pencil, eraser (stationery); Bluetooth earphone, charger (electronics); duck toy, toy car (toys).
OOD objects: Marker, digital watch, spinning top.

5.1.6 pick_items_into_basket

Goal: Pick up four items from the table and place them into a basket.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): For each of 4 items: pick up (1) + place in basket (1.25) = 9 pts →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Toy doll, tissue pack, umbrella, charger, medicine box, water bottle.
OOD objects: Medicine bottle, adapter, toy doll 2, flower bouquet.

5.1.7 pour_water_from_bottle

Goal: Move a cup to the table center, grasp a kettle, pour water into the cup, and return the kettle.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Move cup to center (2) →\to Grasp kettle handle & lift (2) →\to Tilt & pour water (3) →\to Place kettle back (2) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Glass cup (blue, red), paper cup (blue, red), ceramic mug (blue, red).
OOD objects: Plastic cup (green — unseen material + color).

Spatial diversity: Handle direction (L/R) ×\times cup position (6 zones) = 12 combinations.

5.1.8 insert_wireline

Goal: Use bimanual coordination to insert a power cable into a wall socket—left gripper picks up the cable, hands off to the right gripper, which inserts it.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Left gripper picks up cable (3) →\to Right gripper receives cable (3) →\to Insert into socket (3) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: White cable, black cable.
OOD objects: Blue cable (unseen color).

Spatial diversity: Socket position (L/R/C) ×\times cable position (U/M/D) = 9 combinations.

5.1.9 put_stationery_in_case

Goal: Open a pencil case (unzip), place three stationery items inside, then close (zip) the case.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Hold case left side (1) →\to Unzip rightward (1.5) →\to Open case (1) →\to Place pencil (1) →\to Place eraser (1) →\to Place marker (1) →\to Hold case right side (1) →\to Zip leftward (1.5) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Blue/green pencil, eraser type 1/2, blue/black marker.
OOD objects: Fountain pen type 1/2.

5.1.10 put_blocks_to_color

Goal: Place colored blocks onto matching color zones (red block on red paper, yellow on yellow, green on green).

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Place red block on red zone (3) →\to Place yellow block on yellow zone (3) →\to Place green block on green zone (3) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Large/small blocks in red, yellow, blue.
OOD objects: Medium blocks in orange, green (unseen sizes + colors).

Diversity dimensions: 7 (block colors, sizes, positions; color-paper positions, count, arrangement, orientation) — the most diverse task.

5.2 Semantic Reasoning Tasks

5.2.1 sort_headphone

Goal: Find headphones in a clutter pile and place them into the correct storage basket.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Find headphones in clutter (2) →\to Pick up headphones (3) →\to Place in basket (4) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Wired in-ear (black), over-ear (black), wireless Bluetooth (black).
OOD objects: Neckband sport headphone (white — new form factor + new color = compound OOD).

Per-trial configuration:

Trial Headphone Type Color OOD Level
T1–T3 Wired in-ear Black In-domain
T4–T6 Over-ear Black Visual shift
T7–T8 Wireless Bluetooth Black Visual shift
T9–T10 Neckband sport White Semantic OOD

5.2.2 classify_items_as_shape

Goal: Sort objects into three zones based on geometric shape category: cube, sphere, cylinder.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Arrange 1st object (3) →\to Arrange 2nd object (3) →\to Arrange 3rd object (3) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Cylindrical batteries (×\times3), cubic erasers (×\times3), rubber balls (×\times3).
OOD objects: Cylindrical lipstick (×\times3), cubic dice (×\times3), small tennis balls (×\times3).

Semantic diversity: The ordering of shape categories varies across trials (e.g., cube-sphere-cylinder vs. cylinder-cube-sphere), requiring the model to recognize abstract shape concepts rather than memorizing a fixed sorting order.

5.2.3 press_button_in_order

Goal: Read a printed color sequence from a card, then press the corresponding colored buttons in order.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Press 1st button (3) →\to Press 2nd button (3) →\to Press 3rd button (3) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training colors: Pink, yellow, blue, green (24 possible permutations of 3 from 4).
OOD colors: Orange, purple (unseen colors).

Per-trial sequences: T1: Pink-Yellow-Blue; T2: Yellow-Blue-Green; T3: Pink-Green-Blue; T4: Blue-Green-Pink; T5: Green-Pink-Yellow; T6: Green-Blue-Yellow; T7: Pink-Blue-Yellow; T8: Yellow-Blue-Pink; T9: Green-Pink-Blue; T10: Blue-Green-Yellow.

5.2.4 pair_up_items

Goal: Given four items (two pairs), find the matching partner for each displayed item and place it below.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Pick matching item for upper-left (2) →\to Place below (2.5) →\to Pick matching item for upper-right (2) →\to Place below (2.5) →\to Retract arms (1).

Training objects: Glove 1–3, sock 1–2 (different colors and patterns).
OOD objects: Glove 4–5, sock 3 (unseen patterns).

5.2.5 pick_fruits_into_basket

Goal: Identify fruits on the table (among distractors like bread and lettuce) and place only the fruits into a basket.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts, variable): When 3 fruits: place each (3 pts each) + retract (1). When 2 fruits: place each (4 pts each) + retract (2). Penalty: −1-1 per non-fruit item placed.

Training objects: Apple, pear, banana, grape; distractors: bread, lettuce; basket 1/2.
OOD objects: Orange, cherry; distractor: small toy doll; basket 3.

5.3 Mobile Manipulation Tasks

5.3.1 put_clothes_in_hamper

Goal: Navigate to a sofa, pick up clothing items (shirt, pants, socks), carry them to a hamper, and place them inside. Requires three round-trips.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Navigate to shirt (0.5) →\to Pick shirt (1) →\to Navigate to hamper (0.5) →\to Place shirt (1) →\to Navigate to pants (0.5) →\to Pick pants (1) →\to Navigate to hamper (0.5) →\to Place pants (1) →\to Navigate to socks (0.5) →\to Pick left sock (1) →\to Pick right sock (1) →\to Navigate to hamper (0.5) →\to Place socks (0.5) →\to Retract arms (0.5). 14 sub-tasks, avg 193.6 s.

Training objects: Shirt type 1/2, pants type 1/2, socks type 1/2.
OOD objects: Shirt 3, pants 3, socks 3.

5.3.2 hang_up_picture

Goal: Navigate to a shelf, pick up a painting with both hands, carry it to a hanging board, and hang it.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Navigate to shelf (1) →\to Bimanual pick painting (3) →\to Navigate to board (1) →\to Raise painting (2) →\to Hang on board (2) →\to Retract arms (1). Avg 142.6 s.

Training objects: Large painting, small painting.
OOD objects: Medium painting.

5.3.3 organize_shoes

Goal: Navigate to scattered shoes, pick up a pair (left and right), carry to a shoe rack, and place neatly.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Navigate to shoes (1) →\to Pick left shoe (2) →\to Pick right shoe (2) →\to Navigate to rack (1) →\to Place left shoe (1.5) →\to Place right shoe (1.5) →\to Retract arms (1). Avg 96.4 s.

Training objects: Slippers type 1, men’s shoes type 1, women’s shoes type 1.
OOD objects: Slippers 2, men’s shoes 2, women’s shoes 2.

5.3.4 put_bottle_on_woodshelf

Goal: Navigate to a table, pick up a bottle, navigate to a shelf, and place it.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Navigate to table (2) →\to Pick up bottle (2) →\to Navigate to shelf (2) →\to Place on shelf (2) →\to Retract arms (2). Avg 93.7 s.

Training objects: Water bottle, Coke plastic bottle.
OOD objects: Aluminum can, plastic vase.

5.3.5 take_and_set_tableware

Goal: Navigate to a shelf, pick up a basket of utensils, carry to a table, then set the table: place plate on napkin, knife to the left, fork to the right.

Sub-task scoring (10 pts): Navigate to shelf (1) →\to Bimanual pick basket (1) →\to Navigate to table (1) →\to Place basket right of napkin (1) →\to Place plate on napkin (1) →\to Place knife left of plate (2) →\to Place fork right of plate (2) →\to Retract arms (1). Avg ∼\sim211 s.

Training objects: Metal knife/fork, ceramic plate.
OOD objects: Plastic knife/fork, plastic plate.

6 Training Data Diversity Specifications

Each task is accompanied by a diversity guide specifying the exact object variants, spatial configurations, and compositional permutations to be covered during data collection. Table 5 summarizes all diversity dimensions.

Collection protocol. For each task, trained operators follow the diversity guide to collect trajectories (range: 451–645 per task, 10,812 total). Each diversity dimension is kept approximately uniformly distributed (within 10–15% of equal frequency) to prevent models from exploiting distribution biases. Data collection spanned 28 days across 5 robot units, with quality checks to filter failed demonstrations.

7 OOD Evaluation Specifications

ManipArena’s evaluation probes generalization along multiple dimensions. For 7 of the 15 tabletop tasks, T9–T10 introduce objects never seen during training (true object-level OOD). For the remaining 8 tasks, T9–T10 vary spatial or compositional configurations within the training distribution (configuration-level generalization). Table 6 provides the complete design.

Semantic distance design. For the 7 tasks with true OOD, objects are chosen at varying semantic distances from the training distribution:

  • •

    Near-OOD: Safety goggles (for put_glasses) — similar overall shape, same grasp strategy applicable.

  • •

    Medium-OOD: Bluetooth earbuds (for sort_headphone) — different form factor, same functional category; sunglasses (for put_glasses) — similar shape, different folding.

  • •

    Far-OOD: Neckband headphones (for sort_headphone) — radically different form + white color = compound shift; black plastic spoon (for put_spoon) — both material and color changed simultaneously.

8 Sensor and Action Space Specification

8.1 Tabletop Tasks (56D)

Each frame of tabletop task data contains 56-dimensional state and action vectors for the bimanual follow arms:

8.2 Mobile Tasks (62D)

Mobile manipulation tasks include all 56 dimensions above plus 6 additional dimensions for the mobile base:

8.3 Data Collection

The full data collection records 112D per frame (follow + master arms for both sides). The open-source release provides only the follow-arm subset (56D tabletop / 62D mobile) for direct use in policy training. Coordinate convention: xx increases forward, yy increases left, zz increases upward.

8.4 Camera Views

Three RGB cameras at 20 fps, resolution 640×\times480:

  • •

    Face camera (faceImg): Front-facing, captures the global workspace layout.

  • •

    Left wrist camera (leftImg): Mounted on the left arm’s end-effector.

  • •

    Right wrist camera (rightImg): Mounted on the right arm’s end-effector.
